tanattu.title: “Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me”: moderation between excess and neglect
participants: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
tanattu.eventDescription: Three Companions came to the houses of the Prophet's ﷺ wives asking about his private worship. When they were told, they seemed to consider it little. One said: As for me, I will pray all night and never stop. Another said: I will fast every day and never break my fast. The third said: I will never marry. When this reached the Prophet ﷺ he came to them and said: “Are you the ones who said such and such? By Allah, I am the most fearful of Allah among you and the most conscious of Him, yet I fast and break my fast, I pray and I sleep, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.”
tanattu.historicalContext: One of the foundational hadith establishing the Islamic method of moderation; scholars used it as a basis in responding to extremism and excessive strictness in religion.
tanattu.problemType: Wanting to be extremely strict, religiously or otherwise, believing it proves greater seriousness or commitment
tanattu.responseType: Directly correcting the idea, and linking the true example to balance rather than strictness
emotionsAddressed: Guilt for not reaching an ideal level of commitment
The urge to prove seriousness through strictness or self-deprivation
principles: The highest level of commitment does not mean the greatest deprivation or strictness
Whoever goes beyond the example's guidance in the name of piety leaves the right way rather than adding to it
Balance between life's different areas is the sound way, not the exception
modernApplications: If you find yourself overdoing one area (work, worship, sport, study) until you neglect others, remember that balance is the goal, not extremes
Do not measure your seriousness by how much you deprive yourself, but by your consistency and balance
Beware of the popular “extreme achievement” messages that glorify exhaustion as proof of seriousness
notToApplyTo: This does not mean not striving in worship or work, but avoiding the excess that leads to burnout or giving up
behaviorObservations: He did not rebuke them harshly, though their intention was good
He presented himself as a model of moderation, not strictness, although he was the most fearful of Allah
He linked leaving his balanced way with leaving his method, not with extra religiosity
whatToAvoid: Thinking that excessive deprivation of lawful things is a sign of superiority or higher piety
tanattu.reflection: The highest example was not found in the most severe deprivation, but in the most complete balance.
keywords: i'm exhausted from too many commitments
i want to be stricter with myself
i feel guilty for not achieving perfectly
i deprived myself of everything to be better
i cancelled my social life to achieve
burnout from too much worship or work

quranRefs.context: A Quranic description of this nation as “a middle nation” — a nation of moderation and justice between excess and neglect
quranRefs.relevance: It establishes moderation as the collective identity of the nation, not just guidance for one individual situation as in the hadith

hadithRefs.narrator: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him)

muadh-taweel.title: “Are you causing trouble, Mu‘adh?”: considering those who follow you
participants: Mu‘adh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him)
muadh-taweel.eventDescription: Mu‘adh ibn Jabal used to pray the night prayer behind the Prophet ﷺ, then go and lead his own people in it again. One night he made the recitation very long, and a man behind him left and finished his prayer alone, because he worked all day. Mu‘adh was angry at his leaving and accused him of hypocrisy. The man came complaining to the Prophet ﷺ, who was angry at what Mu‘adh had done and said to him: “Are you causing trouble, Mu‘adh?” — three times — “Why didn't you recite ‘Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High’ and ‘By the sun and its brightness’ and the like? For behind you pray the old, the weak and those with needs.”
muadh-taweel.historicalContext: One of the foundational hadith on leading prayer and considering the circumstances of those you lead; agreed to be authentic.
muadh-taweel.problemType: Someone in a leadership position imposing a high standard with good intentions, without considering the abilities of those they lead
muadh-taweel.responseType: Clear anger at ignoring others' needs, and direct practical guidance to correct the approach
emotionsAddressed: Frustration with a leader or manager who does not consider your circumstances
Guilt at not keeping up with a high standard imposed by others
principles: Good intentions are not enough to justify ignoring the needs of those you lead
A good leader sets the standard by the weakest follower, not by personal ambition
Accusing someone unable to keep up with a high standard of failing is clear injustice
modernApplications: If you are responsible for a team, set your expectations by the ability of the weakest, not the strongest
Do not assume that someone who cannot keep up with your high standard is failing; their circumstances may be different
Ask for feedback from those you lead and listen to their complaints, as the Prophet ﷺ listened to that man's complaint
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ was clearly angry that Mu‘adh ignored the worshippers' needs, even though he meant no harm
He offered a specific practical alternative instead of only blaming
He listened to a simple man's complaint against a figure of Mu‘adh's standing
whatToAvoid: Blaming without offering a practical alternative
muadh-taweel.reflection: Sometimes excessive eagerness for the best is itself what drives away the very people you want to benefit.
keywords: my boss imposes exhausting standards on the team
my manager doesn't consider our circumstances
a teacher drags the lesson on without considering students
a leader who doesn't consider those he leads

hadithRefs.narrator: Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with them)

contrasts: Here he strongly reproached someone who erred with good intentions towards the weak; there he was patient with the rudeness of someone with a clear right — the measure is the act's effect on others, not the doer's intention alone

bayyian-khiyar.title: Buyer and seller have the option: blessing lies in honesty, not quick profit
participants: Hakim ibn Hizam (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
bayyian-khiyar.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ established a basic principle of trade ethics, saying: “The buyer and seller have the option as long as they have not parted. If they are truthful and make things clear, their transaction will be blessed; and if they lie and conceal, the blessing of their transaction will be wiped out,” linking honesty and transparency in dealings to real blessing in earnings, not merely apparent profit.
bayyian-khiyar.historicalContext: One of the foundational hadith on financial and commercial dealings; agreed to be authentic.
bayyian-khiyar.problemType: The temptation to make a quicker profit by hiding information or exaggerating a product or service
bayyian-khiyar.responseType: Linking honesty and transparency in dealings to something deeper than material profit: “blessing”
emotionsAddressed: The temptation to lie or conceal to get a better deal
Anxiety about losing a deal because of full transparency
principles: Honesty and transparency in trade directly bring blessing; they are not an obstacle to profit
Concealment and lying may bring quick apparent profit but take away the real blessing
Each party's right to full knowledge before completing a deal is an essential part of commercial justice
modernApplications: Be completely transparent about the defects or limits of what you sell or the service you offer, even if it costs you a deal
Do not measure a deal's or a job's success by immediate profit alone, but by the honesty it was built on
Give the other party a real chance to know everything they need before committing
behaviorObservations: He linked “the option” to both parties' right to full knowledge before final commitment
He used the concept of “blessing”, not only lawful and unlawful, to show an extra dimension of honesty
whatToAvoid: Thinking that commercial honesty necessarily means losing the deal; the text links it to blessing, not loss
bayyian-khiyar.reflection: When the measure of success becomes blessing rather than profit alone, every calculation in daily dealings changes.
keywords: should i tell the customer about a defect in the product
temptation not to tell the whole truth in a deal
how to be honest in my business
the customer won't buy if he knows the whole truth

hadithRefs.narrator: Hakim ibn Hizam (may Allah be pleased with him)

tabassum-sadaqa.title: Your smile to your brother is charity: the greatness of small deeds
participants: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
tabassum-sadaqa.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ widened the idea of “charity” to include simple daily acts that cost no money. He said to Abu Dharr: “Your smiling in your brother's face is charity for you; your enjoining good and forbidding evil is charity; your guiding a man in a land where he is lost is charity; your helping a man with poor sight to see is charity; your removing a stone, a thorn or a bone from the road is charity; and your pouring from your bucket into your brother's bucket is charity.”
tabassum-sadaqa.historicalContext: One of the hadith that widen the concept of good deeds to include simple daily details, not only major acts.
tabassum-sadaqa.problemType: Feeling unable to “do good” because of lack of time or money
tabassum-sadaqa.responseType: Redefining good deeds to include simple daily acts within everyone's reach
emotionsAddressed: Feeling inadequate for not being able to give money or do great deeds
Belittling small acts like a smile or simple help
principles: Good is not reserved for those with lots of money or time
Small repeated acts have real value, not just symbolic value
Widening the meaning of “charity” makes doing good possible every day, not a rare occasion
modernApplications: Do not belittle the effect of a sincere smile or a kind word you say today
Look for small opportunities for good in your day instead of waiting for a big one
If you feel inadequate because you cannot give money, remember that the doors of good are far wider than that
behaviorObservations: He listed varied examples from daily life, not just one
He put the value of a smile alongside other deeds that seem greater, such as enjoining good
whatToAvoid: Settling for small acts as a substitute for greater giving when you are able
tabassum-sadaqa.reflection: When the circle of “charity” widens to include a smile, doing good becomes within every person's reach at every moment.
keywords: i feel i don't do enough good
i have no money to give in charity
how to do good without money
i feel i fall short in doing good

umm-salama-dua.title: “To Allah we belong and to Him we return”: a supplication that turns calamity into hope
participants: Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her)
umm-salama-dua.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ taught his Companions a practical supplication for times of calamity: “There is no servant struck by a calamity who says: ‘To Allah we belong and to Him we will return. O Allah, reward me in my calamity and replace it for me with something better,’ except that Allah rewards him in his calamity and replaces it with something better.” Umm Salamah applied this supplication herself after the death of her husband Abu Salamah, despite wondering inwardly: “Who could be better for me than Abu Salamah?” Later the Prophet ﷺ married her, and she became a living proof of what she had prayed for.
umm-salama-dua.historicalContext: One of the hadith combining instruction (the supplication) with practice (Umm Salamah's own story) in dealing with the loss of a spouse.
umm-salama-dua.problemType: Losing a spouse or a loved one, and despairing of ever getting past the loss
umm-salama-dua.responseType: Teaching a specific practical supplication combining submission to Allah with asking for future good
emotionsAddressed: Despair after losing a spouse or someone very dear
Doubting that any good could come after this particular loss
principles: Supplication in calamity is not just words; it turns the heart towards hope, not only despair
Doubting that “good is coming” is natural and human, and does not contradict saying the supplication sincerely
Submission to Allah's decree and asking for the future meet in the same supplication
modernApplications: After losing someone very dear, allow yourself to doubt that there could be a “replacement” without letting that stop you from praying and hoping
Practise this supplication as a concrete step in calamity, not just traditional words
Remember Umm Salamah's story when hope seems completely out of reach; the good to come may be beyond what you can now imagine
notToApplyTo: This does not mean every calamity will necessarily be followed by a similar replacement in this world; the promised good may be in this life or the next
behaviorObservations: He taught a specific practical supplication, not just general advice to be patient
She did not hide that she applied it despite her honest inner doubt when she said it
whatToAvoid: Hastily preaching to someone who lost their spouse that “Allah will replace it” without first giving them space to grieve
umm-salama-dua.reflection: Umm Salamah's story is a rare embodiment of a supplication fulfilled literally, reminding us that hope has meaning even when it seems unimaginable.
keywords: is there any good after this loss
my husband died and i can't imagine life without him

quranRefs.context: This verse is the direct Quranic source of the phrase “To Allah we belong and to Him we will return”, which the Prophet ﷺ taught his Companions to say
quranRefs.relevance: It links saying these words to the description of the patient who are given glad tidings of blessings and mercy from their Lord, as in the very next verse

hadithRefs.narrator: Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her)

jasad-wahid.title: Like one body: the mutual care of the believers
participants: al-Nu‘man ibn Bashir (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
jasad-wahid.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ compared the social bonds between believers to a single human body, saying: “You see the believers in their mercy, love and sympathy for one another like one body: when one part of it complains, the rest of the body responds with sleeplessness and fever,” showing that the suffering of any member of the community should be felt by all, not left to them alone.
jasad-wahid.historicalContext: One of the comprehensive hadith describing the ideal social bond between members of a community.
jasad-wahid.problemType: Indifference to the suffering of others in your community or circle, on the grounds that it is “not my problem”
jasad-wahid.responseType: A powerful comparison that makes an individual's suffering a shared concern, not an isolated one
emotionsAddressed: Indifference or detachment from the suffering of those around you
Loneliness when going through hardship and feeling no one is affected
principles: In a connected community, anyone's suffering calls for a response from all, not neglect
Real social bonds show in moments of pain, not only in times of ease
The body comparison shows that neglect harms the whole body; it is not a neutral choice
modernApplications: When someone in your circle is going through hardship, do not settle for silent sympathy; take real action
Ask yourself: do I treat those around me as one body, or as separate, unconnected individuals?
If you are struggling and feel alone, remember that asking your circle for support is a right, not a weakness
behaviorObservations: He used a physical image (the body) for an abstract concept (social bonds) to bring it closer to understanding
whatToAvoid: Understanding solidarity as excessive interference in others' privacy rather than balanced support
jasad-wahid.reflection: When an individual feels their pain concerns the whole community, belonging becomes a living meaning, not an empty slogan.
keywords: i feel no one cares about my problem
how to build a caring community
my friends don't respond to my worries

quranRefs.context: The Quranic basis of the brotherhood of faith on which the hadith's image of one body rests
quranRefs.relevance: It establishes that faith itself is brotherhood, and that reconciling between believers is a condition for receiving mercy

hadithRefs.narrator: al-Nu‘man ibn Bashir (may Allah be pleased with them)

birr-walidayn.title: Your mother, then your mother, then your mother, then your father: the priority of honouring parents
participants: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
birr-walidayn.eventDescription: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked: Who among people is most deserving of my good companionship? The Prophet ﷺ said: “Your mother.” He asked: Then who? He said: “Your mother.” He asked: Then who? He said: “Your mother.” He asked: Then who? He said: “Your father,” affirming the mother's priority in kindness three times over the father, because of the hardship she bore in pregnancy, birth and nursing.
birr-walidayn.historicalContext: One of the foundational hadith on the priorities of honouring parents; agreed to be authentic.
birr-walidayn.problemType: Questions about priorities in honouring parents, or neglecting one of them because of busyness
birr-walidayn.responseType: Repeating the answer three times to highlight the mother's particular priority in kindness
emotionsAddressed: Feeling one falls short towards one's parents amid life's demands
Uncertainty about how to divide time and attention between the parents
principles: Honouring the mother deserves exceptional care because of what she bore in pregnancy, nursing and upbringing
Repetition in the answer is a Prophetic way of highlighting the importance of something
Honouring parents is not one equal duty; it has priorities and details
modernApplications: Set aside real time and attention for your mother specifically, not just general kindness to your parents
If you are very busy, set your priorities so honouring your parents stays at the top, not the margins
Do not wait for a special occasion to show your kindness; simple daily care is the foundation
notToApplyTo: This does not mean neglecting the father's right, but putting the mother first in priority within honouring both
behaviorObservations: He repeated the same answer three times in a row before mentioning the father
He did not settle for a general answer (“honour your parents”) but set a clear priority
whatToAvoid: Understanding this hadith as diminishing the father's right
birr-walidayn.reflection: When the same answer is repeated three times, it becomes clear that some rights deserve emphasis, not just a mention.
keywords: i feel i fall short towards my parents
how to balance honouring my mother and father

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)

ghirah-aisha.title: ‘A'ishah's jealousy of Khadijah: respecting feelings without giving up loyalty
ghirah-aisha.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ often spoke well of his first wife Khadijah after her death. ‘A'ishah — despite her special place with him — felt jealous of how often he mentioned her, until one day she reproached him. The Prophet's ﷺ face changed and he defended his loyalty to Khadijah's memory, admitting his honest feelings: “I was blessed with her love.”
ghirah-aisha.historicalContext: One of the hadith revealing the human side of the Prophet's ﷺ married life, and the balance between loyalty to the memory of someone who has died and respect for the feelings of the current spouse.
ghirah-aisha.problemType: A spouse's jealousy of the memory of a previous relationship or an important person in the other's life
ghirah-aisha.responseType: Complete honesty about feelings, without a courtesy that would give up the duty of loyalty to the previous person's memory
emotionsAddressed: Jealousy of the memory of someone from a partner's past
Wanting to hear insincere reassurance to calm jealousy
principles: Honest expression of feelings is better than a temporary courtesy that drops the value of loyalty
Loyalty to the memory of someone who has died does not necessarily diminish the current relationship
Jealousy is a natural human feeling that does not deserve harsh blame
modernApplications: Do not expect your partner to completely deny the value of an important past relationship or memory to please you; honesty matters more than courtesy
If you feel jealous of someone from the past, express it openly as ‘A'ishah did, without asking for the truth to be denied
Loyalty to the past and love for the present can coexist without contradiction
behaviorObservations: He did not give up acknowledging his love for Khadijah to please ‘A'ishah
He did not blame ‘A'ishah for her jealousy despite her direct reproach
He combined honesty about his feelings with tenderness towards ‘A'ishah's
whatToAvoid: Thinking jealousy is settled by denying a truth or a past
ghirah-aisha.reflection: Sometimes the most honest cure for jealousy is complete honesty, not a denial that is comfortable for the moment.
keywords: i'm jealous of my partner's past
my husband mentions someone important from his past and i get jealous
how to deal with my jealousy

khullah-abu-bakr.title: “If I were to take a close friend”: the value of true friendship
participants: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him)
khullah-abu-bakr.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ described his relationship with his closest friend, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, in eloquent words: “If I were to take a close friend (khalil) from my nation, I would take Abu Bakr; but he is my brother and my companion,” showing that Abu Bakr's place with him did not come from nothing, but from long companionship and support with his wealth and himself in the hardest stages.
khullah-abu-bakr.historicalContext: This statement appears in more than one place in the biography, and it is one of the clearest texts on Abu Bakr's high standing.
khullah-abu-bakr.problemType: Undervaluing a long, sincere friendship, or not openly acknowledging a close friend's place
khullah-abu-bakr.responseType: Explicit, public acknowledgement of the friend's special standing
emotionsAddressed: Hesitation to openly express appreciation for a close friend
Feeling that friendships do not deserve the same attention as family ties
principles: Friendship built on long companionship and real support deserves explicit, not implicit, acknowledgement
Those closest to you are often the ones who supported you in the hardest moments, not those closest by blood
Openly expressing appreciation for friends strengthens social bonds
modernApplications: Do not hesitate to openly express your appreciation for a friend who supported you through hard times
Judge your friendships by sincerity and real support, not by number of acquaintances
Take time to appreciate those who stood by you when others turned their backs
behaviorObservations: He chose a strong, specific word (“khalil”) rather than a general description
He tied the standing to a clear reason — long companionship and support — not empty flattery
khullah-abu-bakr.reflection: When friendship is built on sincere support in the hardest times, it deserves acknowledgement no less explicit than any other relationship.
keywords: how to express appreciation to my friend
a friend who stood by me in the hardest times

hadithRefs.narrator: ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud (may Allah be pleased with him)

gharib-dunya.title: “Be in this world as a stranger”: living with awareness and intention, not attachment
participants: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (may Allah be pleased with them)
gharib-dunya.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ took hold of ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar's shoulder and advised him: “Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a traveller passing through.” Ibn ‘Umar understood this practically and used to say: “When evening comes, do not wait for the morning; when morning comes, do not wait for the evening. Take from your health for your illness, and from your life for your death.”
gharib-dunya.historicalContext: One of the comprehensive hadith guiding towards living with awareness and purpose, without excessive attachment that makes a person forget how limited their time is.
gharib-dunya.problemType: Constant procrastination or excessive attachment to temporary worldly things at the expense of what matters more
gharib-dunya.responseType: An eloquent image (the stranger/traveller) that reshapes one's relationship with time and possessions
emotionsAddressed: Feeling that time is unlimited, so everything important gets postponed
Existential anxiety about mortality when facing it directly
principles: Awareness of limited time drives action, not despair
Excessive attachment to this world as a permanent home makes one forget its temporary nature
Using times of strength to prepare for times of weakness is a practical method, not just philosophy
modernApplications: Stop postponing important things on the grounds that “there's plenty of time”; time is shorter than it seems
Use your times of strength, health and energy to build what will benefit you when you weaken
Reduce excessive attachment to temporary details and focus on what will leave a lasting effect
notToApplyTo: This does not mean neglecting planning for the future or not building a stable life; the point is not excessive attachment, not lack of preparation
behaviorObservations: He used a physical touch (holding the shoulder) to emphasise the importance of the advice
Ibn ‘Umar did not just memorise the words but turned them into a clear daily practice
whatToAvoid: Turning this meaning into constant anxiety about death instead of a positive motivation to act
gharib-dunya.reflection: When you see yourself as a traveller passing through rather than a permanent resident, everything you consider “important” in your day changes.
keywords: i feel there isn't enough time
how to make better use of my time and health

hadithRefs.narrator: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (may Allah be pleased with them)
